1.title: Fact and Dimension Tables, Merge, Append and Load
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Fact and Dimension Tables, Merge, Append and Load. It covers the exam area Prepare the data. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Create fact tables and dimension tables. Identify when to use reference or duplicate queries and the resulting impact. Merge and append queries. Identify and create appropriate keys for relationships. Configure data loading for queries. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Prepare the data (twenty-five-thirty percent). Exam format: a one hundred-minute proctored exam; a score of seven hundred on a scale to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official P L three hundred study guide, skills measured as of April twenty, twenty twenty-six.

1.title: Create fact tables and dimension tables
1.text: Create fact tables and dimension tables. A star schema puts a fact table in the middle and dimension tables around it. Power B I models run best on this shape.

1.title: Create fact tables and dimension tables, continued
1.text: Create fact tables and dimension tables. The figure shows this: A star schema has a fact table in the middle and dimension tables around it, each linked by a one-to-many relationship.

1.title: Create fact tables and dimension tables, continued
1.text: Create fact tables and dimension tables. Dimension. Holds: Descriptions of an entity: product, customer, date, store. Used to: Filter and group. Fact. Holds: Events such as sales lines: dimension keys and numeric columns. Used to: Summarize. The rules to remember. Relationships run one-to-many from the dimension (one side) to the fact (many side). A fact table has one consistent grain, for example one row per order line. Do not mix dimension columns and fact columns in one table. A snowflake of linked dimensions can work, but one denormalized dimension is preferred, because a hierarchy cannot span tables.

1.title: Create fact tables and dimension tables, continued
1.text: Create fact tables and dimension tables. A junk dimension holds small flags with few values, a degenerate dimension keeps an order number in the fact table, and a factless fact table records events with no numbers. To build the tables from a flat table, load the flat query once, then make one query per table from it. For a dimension, keep the descriptive columns and the key, then use Remove Duplicates on the key so each row appears once. For the fact table, keep the keys and the numeric columns and remove the descriptions. Exam tip: Dimension tables filter and group, fact tables hold keys and numbers, and the relationship runs one-to-many from the dimension to the fact. Keep one grain per fact table.

1.title: Reference or Duplicate queries
1.text: Reference or Duplicate queries. Both commands are on the right-click menu of a query. They look alike, but they behave differently. What it creates. Reference: A new query whose first step reads the output of the original. Duplicate: A copy of all the steps of the original. Link to the original. Reference: Follows it: a change in the original flows through. Duplicate: Independent: later changes do not reach the copy.

1.title: Reference or Duplicate queries, continued
1.text: Reference or Duplicate queries. Maintenance. Reference: The shared cleaning steps live in one place. Duplicate: Each copy must be changed separately. Use it for. Reference: Fact and dimension tables built from one flat query. Duplicate: A variation you want to change freely.

1.title: Reference or Duplicate queries, continued
1.text: Reference or Duplicate queries. The impact of a Reference: if the original query breaks, for example when a column it uses disappears, every query that references it breaks too. The Query Dependencies view on the View tab shows which query depends on which. A common pattern is a staging query that loads and cleans the flat table, with Reference queries for each dimension and the fact table. Then you disable load on the staging query (section five). Exam tip: Reference follows the original query, and Duplicate is an independent copy of the steps. When cleaning steps change often and every derived table must pick up the change, choose Reference.

1.title: Merge and append queries
1.text: Merge and append queries. Merge adds columns by matching rows. Append adds rows by stacking tables. Both are on the Home tab, in the Combine group. For a merge, select the matching column in each query, and hold Ctrl to select several columns for a combined match. Pick a join kind, then use the expand button on the new column to choose the columns to bring in.

1.title: Merge and append queries, continued
1.text: Merge and append queries. Left Outer. All rows from the first table and matching rows from the second. Right Outer. All rows from the second table and matching rows from the first. Full Outer. All rows from both tables. Inner. Only matching rows. Left Anti. Rows only in the first table, with no match in the second. Right Anti. Rows only in the second table, with no match in the first.

1.title: Merge and append queries, continued
1.text: Merge and append queries. Matching is exact: case and spaces matter, so clean the key columns first. If the second table has duplicate keys, a left outer merge repeats rows from the first table. Merge Queries as New keeps the originals and creates a new query. Append Queries stacks rows from two tables or three or more tables. Columns are matched by name, and a column missing in one table is filled with null. Append Queries as New creates a new query and leaves the originals unchanged. Use it for monthly tables with the same layout.

1.title: Merge and append queries, continued
1.text: Merge and append queries. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: Merge adds columns and append adds rows. Left Anti returns rows in the first table that have no match in the second, which finds missing or orphan keys.

1.title: Create appropriate keys for relationships
1.text: Create appropriate keys for relationships. A relationship needs a single column on the one side whose values are unique. If the one-side column has duplicate values, the model refresh fails. The two key columns need matching data types.

1.title: Create appropriate keys for relationships, continued
1.text: Create appropriate keys for relationships. The key repeats in the dimension. Remove Duplicates on the key to make one row per value. There is no usable key. Add an Index Column to the dimension as a surrogate key, then bring it into the fact table with a merge. The match needs several columns. Create a composite key: Merge Columns with a separator, in both tables, in the same format. Power B I relationships use one column on each side. That is why two columns that identify a row together must be combined into one key first.

2.title: Create appropriate keys for relationships, continued
2.text: Create appropriate keys for relationships. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: The one side of a relationship needs a unique column; duplicates make refresh fail. Create a surrogate key with an index column, and a composite key by merging columns.

2.title: Configure data loading for queries
2.text: Configure data loading for queries. Each query has settings on its right-click menu in the Queries pane. They decide what ends up in the model. Enable load. On: the query becomes a table in the model. Off: it only runs when other queries use it. Include in report refresh. Off: Refresh and scheduled refresh skip this query's data. Close and Apply. Sends the results to the model and closes the editor; Apply keeps the editor open.

2.title: Configure data loading for queries, continued
2.text: Configure data loading for queries. Disable load for staging and intermediate queries, such as the flat table that other queries reference. They then stay out of the model, which keeps it smaller. A query that is not loaded still runs when a referencing query needs it. Turn off Include in report refresh only for data that should not change, such as a fixed lookup list. Queries load in parallel, so the load order is not guaranteed. Never rely on one query loading before another. Express dependencies with Reference instead. Exam tip: Clear Enable load on staging queries so they do not become model tables. Hiding a table in Report view is different: a hidden table is still loaded.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A flat Orders query is cleaned in several steps that change often. The Product and Sales queries must always pick up those changes. What should the analyst create? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Reference queries of Orders, which follow its output. A Reference starts from the output of the original, so changes in the original flow through.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A flat Sales table holds Product I D, Product Name, Category, Amount and Quantity. Which columns belong in the Product dimension table? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Product I D, Product Name and Category. A dimension holds the key and the descriptive columns, while Amount and Quantity belong in the fact table.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. An analyst must list the customers in the Customer table who have no rows in the Sales table. Which join kind should the merge use, with Customer as the first table? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Left Anti, which keeps rows only in the first table. Left Anti returns the first-table rows that have no match in the second.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Twelve monthly tables have the same columns, and the analyst needs one table with all rows. The originals must stay unchanged. Which command should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Append Queries as New, with three or more tables. Append Queries as New stacks the rows of many tables into a new query and leaves the originals unchanged.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Two tables relate by Store and Date together, but Power B I relationships use one column. What should the analyst do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Create a combined key column in both tables. Merging the two columns into one composite key in both tables gives each relationship a single column to match.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A flat Orders query is referenced by the Product and Sales queries. How do you keep Orders from becoming a table in the model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Clear Enable load for the Orders query. Clearing Enable load keeps the query out of the model while the referencing queries still use it.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the difference between Reference and Duplicate? Answer: Reference follows the original query, and Duplicate is an independent copy of its steps. Question two. Which join kind returns all rows from both tables? Answer: Full Outer. Question three. How do you create a surrogate key? Answer: Add an Index Column to the deduplicated dimension.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Does merge add rows or columns, and does append add rows or columns? Answer: Merge adds columns, and append adds rows. Question five. Is the load order of queries guaranteed? Answer: No, queries load in parallel. Question six. In which direction does a star schema relationship run? Answer: One-to-many, from the dimension to the fact table.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Star schema: dimensions filter and group; facts hold keys and numbers; one-to-many from dimension to fact. Reference: follows the original; changes flow through; one place to maintain. Duplicate: independent copy of the steps; later changes do not reach it. Merge: adds columns; Left Outer, Right Outer, Full Outer, Inner, Left Anti, Right Anti. Append: adds rows; two tables or three or more; matched by name. Keys: unique one side; Remove Duplicates; Index Column as surrogate key. Loading: Enable load off for staging; Include in report refresh; Close and Apply.
